unplaced.en: (a) 'Both alone and impassible.' This is certainly so as regards the merit and inclination of divine charity; but since in our present state we do not have it in such a way that it fully subjects all our motions to itself (the highest and universal Good not yet being beheld in itself, and infinite not only for itself but for us), it follows that all our impassibility, which Maximus and other Orthodox celebrate, is only a kind of beginning of that true impassibility we await, with perfect union with God and charity now full-grown; it is not truly sinlessness itself, [...] and unless by God's help we cannot merely avoid sinning but can altogether not sin; whatever those whom Jerome in this connection harries as Origenist monks may have thought, and whom Theophilus pursued still more harshly; after whose excess, their motions being quieted, the Christian impassibility of ours seemed rather to flourish through the deserts of Egypt and Nitria, than that inaccessible and Stoic one of Christ's grace.

Habet et vim quamdam cessandi, quod qui metu comprimuntur, nec movere se, nec mussitare audent. Sic itaque in inferni barathro pavidi semper reprobi, quæ illis tristitia maxima et mœror. Τὸ πήξεως, communius est, magisque respiciat inanima; nec tam στυγνότητα legendum, quam στενότητα: ut fixæ tartari angustiis morae injucunditas designaretur; quod voluisse videbatur Dufrenii Antiquarius in illa voce parum depravata, στεγνότητα, non explicato motu proprio viventium, ex mali imminentis cum stupore certa exspectatione.
unplaced.anchorLine: … ἀφανισθέντα ... στυγνότητα πτήξεως (c), τῶν ἐκουσίων ἡμῶν κακῶν
unplaced.en: (c) 'And the gloominess of cowering.' I rightly prefer this reading of the Venetian codex, because it gives a clear sense, and the word so used (πτῆξις) is not repugnant to the punishment of the prison of hell. For τὸ πτήσσειν, they say, is properly said of animals which, seeing the enemy, dare not come out but through fear crouch down in some suitable place to hide. It also has a certain force of ceasing, since those held down by fear dare neither move nor mutter. So in the pit of hell the reprobate are ever fearful, and theirs is the greatest sadness and grief. [The word] πήξεως is more general and looks rather to inanimate things; and στυγνότητα should not be read so much as στενότητα, so that the unpleasantness of delay in the narrow straits of fixed Tartarus would be indicated; which Dufresne's Antiquarius seemed to intend in that somewhat corrupt word στεγνότητα, without explaining the proper movement of living things, from the sure expectation of imminent evil with stupor.

Non satis accurata hæc gratiæ videatur prædicatio, ut hoc solum in Deum reducantur virtutis opera, quod ipse vires ad ea natura indiderit; quæ ipsa inde supra voluntatem animique sententiam primas obtineat, quod non nisi ex naturæ illa bonitate, ea bona exsistat. unplaced.en: This account of grace does not seem accurate enough: it says that the works of virtue are referred to God only because He gave nature the strength for them, so that virtue, springing from that goodness of nature, takes first place above the will and the soul's judgment, since it exists only from nature's own goodness, and is good only so. Pelagius could readily use these very words; but Maximus means nature as established together with gratuitous gifts, such as it was first created in Adam and is restored to us in Christ, which further needs actual aids; without these neither natural nor gratuitous strength would suffice to bring about virtue, or to persevere in it, or to seize its citadel, toward which all that Maximus says earnestly points.

Vulg. proxime Hebr. et desieris extendere digitos; sive quasi ad rapinam mittere: nam et de uncis unguibus interpretantur, quibus aves rapaces in prædam involant, Jer. xii, 9. Χειροτονίαν τῶν LXX hic accipit Maximus, pro delectu, quo sibi quisque alios demerendos præsumit, alios negligit, qua discretione sibi ipse naturam scindit, et ab eleemosynæ et charitatis scopo longius abscedit. Tria ergo hic vitia insinuata, colligatio et catena, ipsa justitiæ violatæ injuria; electio seu delectus, quasi scilicet personarum acceptio; ac demum murmuratio orisque detractio. Longe a vero Nobil. hic ordinationem, τὴν χειροτονίαν reddit, nihilque ad mentem Scripturæ. Dicitur ordinatio in mysteriis usu ecclesiastico, quæ est sacrorum ministrorum manuum impositione consecratio et inauguratio, qualem ex Paulo habemus, non nuda suffragiorum collatione Calviniano ritu electio, uti incaute nimis expressit, qui abs me editam Gr. et Lat. Petri martyris Alexandrini illustrem Vitam, haud ita pridem quasi compendio Gallice reddidit. Nam ubi auctor, Reliquis omnibus legitimis servatis, οὕτως ἐχειροτονήθη: ibi ille, il fut ainsi élu, nempe Achillas presbyter Petri successor: at catholice et ecclesiastice, ex mente scriptoris, il fut ainsi sacré, ordonné: nam nec vocem hanc respuit noster idiotismus: quidquid sit de Ecclesiæ Alexandrinæ ritu, et an vere presbyteri in ea ordinationem haberent episcopi, e quorum cœtu; unus reliquis prælatus, solus episcopus audiret, ad unitatem servandam, et ne qua esset in ea Ecclesia occasio schismatis: cujus rei examen alterius operæ et otii sit, ut et excussio originum Eutychii ejusque interpretum. Quo argumento strenua nuper desudavit opera Joannis Pearson presbyteri Angli, libro Vindiciarum epistolarum S. Ignatii, stramineamque, nullisque antiquitatis luminibus fultam Eutychii hujus recentis hominis ostendit lucubrationem. Ratum interim esse debeat, nihil officere veræ fidei ac disciplinæ, si quid illi Ecclesiæ Eutychii jam ætate obrepserat, et ubi fœdari erroribus et ab Ecclesia Romana ac catholicæ communionis arce discessionem facere olim cœperat.
unplaced.anchorLine: Ἀνέχετε σύνδεσμον καὶ χειροτονίαν (f) καὶ ῥῆμα γογγυσμοῦ
unplaced.en: Combefis: "And ordination" (χειροτονίαν). The Vulgate, close to the Hebrew, reads "and you cease to stretch out your fingers", or as it were to reach out for plunder: for it is also interpreted of hooked claws with which birds of prey swoop on their quarry (Jer. xii, 9). Maximus takes the LXX's χειροτονίαν here for "choosing" (delectus), by which each man presumes to deserve others, neglects others, and by what discrimination divides nature against himself and strays further from the aim of almsgiving and charity. Three vices are thus intimated: binding and chain; the very wrong done to justice; selection or choosing, as if respect of persons; and finally murmuring and slander. Nobilius, far from the truth, renders it here as "ordination", τὴν χειροτονίαν, with nothing of the mind of Scripture. Ordination is said in ecclesiastical usage of the mysteries: the consecration and inauguration of sacred ministers by laying on of hands, such as we have from Paul, not an election by bare collation of votes in the Calvinist manner, as he too carelessly expressed it, who in a compendium recently put into French the illustrious Life of Peter, martyr of Alexandria, edited by me in Greek and Latin. For where the author has "all else duly observed", οὕτως ἐχειροτονήθη, he renders "il fut ainsi élu" (the successor of Peter, Achillas the presbyter); but in a Catholic and ecclesiastical sense, according to the author's mind, "il fut ainsi sacré, ordonné": for our idiom does not reject this word either. Whatever be the rite of the Church of Alexandria, and whether presbyters there truly had ordination by bishops, from whose body one, set above the rest, alone was called bishop to preserve unity and to avoid any occasion of schism there, the examination of that belongs to another work and leisure, as does a sifting of the origins of Eutychius and his interpreters. On that argument John Pearson, an English presbyter, lately laboured vigorously in his book Vindiciae epistolarum S. Ignatii, and showed the work of this recent man Eutychius to be straw, propped on no lights of antiquity. Let it stand meanwhile that it does no harm to the true faith and discipline if something had already crept into that Church of Eutychius with age, and where it had once begun to fall into errors and to secede from the citadel of Roman and Catholic communion.

unplaced.text: Ὅτι ἀσώματός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή. Procedit vel maxime disputatio hæc contra Origenianos, qui sic animam vel corpus, vel corpori semper conjunctam (etsi tenuioris substantiæ, a crasso hoc nostro corpore) existimabant: quod ipsum sic animæ datum velut carcerem volebant. Argumenta omnia Maximi physica sunt: quod se ille non certo sententiam dicere affirmat, sed quasi disputando quærere, Methodium, Basilium, Patresque alios respicit, qui angelos non omnino vacare corpore senserunt, nec proinde animas: pure scilicet igneum et aereum illis assignantes corpus, cujus merito nobis spiritus, pro terrena hac crassa mole, Deo corpora sint, pro illius elevatiore diversique generis spiritalitate. Aliud certe quod Deus, aliud quod angelus et anima spiritus: nec forte alii aliique Patres reipsa diversa senserunt, etsi re nobis obscura (qui ipsa in se spiritalia, ac per illorum species non cognoscimus) tanta diversitate locuti sunt. Certe plena perfectaque ἀοριστία, absolutioque a loco et tempore, Dei propria est, utcunque exponatur locus angelicus; certaque sphæra est quantitatis ejus virtualis, cui comes ipsa substantia est, ac extra quam nisi mutatione et quasi migrando angelus adesse non potest.
unplaced.anchorLine: τοῦ, Ὅτι ἀσώματός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή (i').
unplaced.en: "That the soul is incorporeal." This argument is chiefly directed against the Origenists, who held that the soul is always joined to a body (even if of finer substance than this coarse body of ours), and who took that body to be as it were its prison. All Maximus's arguments are physical: he says he does not assert an opinion with certainty but inquires as if in disputation; he has in view Methodius, Basil and other Fathers, who held that angels are not wholly without body, nor consequently souls, assigning them a fiery and airy body, by reason of which, in comparison with this earthly gross mass, bodies are said to belong to God, and in comparison with its higher and differently-kinded spirituality. God is one thing, angel and soul spirit another; perhaps other Fathers also thought of different things in reality, though obscure to us, since we know spiritual things neither in themselves nor through their species, and so spoke with such diversity. Certainly full and perfect indefiniteness (aoristia), free of place and time, is proper to God, however angelic place be explained; and the sphere of its virtual quantity is certain, whose companion is the substance itself, apart from which an angel cannot be present except by change and, as it were, by migration.

unplaced.text: Τὴν ἀθανασίαν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀφῃρημένοις. Sic ambo Gregorii aliique sancti Aristotelem trahunt in opinionem mortalitatis animorum, quorum certe magna fides est et auctoritas, pro eorum in Græcis Aristotelis atque ejus dogmatis diligentia. Qui utique, si conciliare Aristotelem licuisset, amicum maluissent, quam ut sibi ac catholicæ fidei, in re tanti, tantum adversarium committerent. Ejus ἐνδελέχεια, actusque et perfectio corporis, velut est acuties in ferro, de hominis animo eoque immortali non satis congruat : sanctus doctor tamen serio laboravit vindicando Aristotelem, et ut ejus sanam mentem in opinione de anima immortali assereret : quæ tractatio longam lucubrationem exposceret ; quæ proinde alterius operæ et otii sit. Rite autem Maximus, ex negatione actus proprii et insignientis, qui in anima rationali, actus ipse rationis est, ut scilicet intelligat et velit, ipsius animæ negationem ac interitum colligit : ut perinde sit, sic inertem esse, ac non esse. Quod monachorum, et in illis celebriorum, fuisse hunc errorem deplorat Maximus, hoc admonet, monachos qui simpliciores minusque eruditi sunt, proclivius errore labi, eoque semel imbibito, fere capitosiores esse, qua sibi blandiuntur sanctitatis larva potius, quam ipsa veritate. Atque utinam Maximi hæc duntaxat tempora contingerent, ac, vel quibus ex munere indicta studiorum necessitas, serio illis secundum pietatem navarent operam, non sæculari ambitu turbas fratribus facerent, omniumque diris devoti, mulierculárum favore omni modo comitatui vim facerent, ut majores prælati et antistites, invitis sacris canonibus Patrumque institutis, fierent, qui nec minora replere subsellia, exigui meritis ac scientia nullaque modestia (ut mitissime dicam) digni exsistant !
unplaced.anchorLine: τὴν ἀθανασίαν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀφῃρημένοις (j),
unplaced.en: Thus both Gregories and other saints draw Aristotle into the opinion that souls are mortal; their faith and authority are certainly great, given their diligence in the Greek Aristotle and his teaching. They would surely, had it been possible to reconcile Aristotle, have preferred him as a friend rather than set so great an adversary against themselves and the catholic faith. His entelechy, the actuality and perfection of the body, like the sharpness in iron, does not sufficiently fit man's soul, and an immortal one; yet the holy doctor laboured earnestly in defending Aristotle and in asserting that his sound meaning lay in the opinion on the immortal soul; that treatment would demand long labour, and belongs to another work and leisure. Rightly, then, Maximus, from the negation of the proper and distinguishing act, which in the rational soul is reason itself, namely that it understand and will, infers the negation and perishing of the soul itself, so that it is the same to be inert as not to be. That Maximus laments this error as having been among monks, and the more famous of them, warns that the simpler and less learned monks slip into error more readily and, once it is imbibed, are generally more stubborn, since they flatter themselves with a mask of holiness rather than the truth. And would that only the times of Maximus had such things befall, and that those on whom study was imposed by their office would earnestly devote themselves to it according to piety, not make disturbances for the brothers by worldly ambition, and, cursed by all, by the favour of little women force their way in every manner into the company, so that they become greater prelates and bishops against the sacred canons and institutions of the Fathers, who are unworthy even to fill the lesser seats, of small merit and learning and (to put it mildly) no modesty!

unplaced.en: 'The fabled bird, the phoenix.' Maximus's precision is especially to be praised: almost alone of the Fathers he openly rejects the fable of the phoenix, whereas the rest either mixed it in or at least left the matter in doubt and blended it with common report. Chief among them is Clement of Rome who, in his simplicity of age, in his Epistle to the Corinthians (the only genuine work of his to reach us) uses the example of the phoenix bird as most true; and Photius says that, in writing so, he uses this as an example. The passage of Scripture misunderstood misled Tertullian and Epiphanius; Clement misled Cyril. Maximus rejects the absurdity as rather natural-historical, and takes care in attacking it not to seem a madman to the prudent, who would waste time on a pointless argument. The occasion was the homonymy of the word φοῖνιξ, which the Seventy often used not for the bird but for the palm, which as it were renews itself and sprouts again. Bochart treated this argument at length in vol. 2 of his work on the animals of sacred Scripture, praising thereby Andreas Schottus's Hexaemeron, diatribe 13.

Great are the gifts for which Maximus here commends Sophronius; and is he the man who withstood Cyrus when he proclaimed a new heresy under the guise of union, and condemned the Ecthesis of Heraclius (or rather Sergius), when he became bishop of Jerusalem, John being the author of its condemnation, who after Honorius presided at Rome? It favours this that so great a teacher and champion of the faith, well furnished with a library, dared to contradict Cyrus and was able to obtain the see of the holy city, which Heraclius had lately won back from the Persians. One outstanding work of his survives: the synodical letter which, soon after becoming bishop, he wrote to Honorius, bishop of the city of Rome, and to Sergius of Constantinople: not one letter and another, as John Dallaeus wrongly puts forward in his disputation on the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite or those circulated under his name, but the very same which Photius held to be addressed to Honorius, and which the Fathers of the Sixth Synod say was addressed to Sergius, as is customary in such encyclicals. Nor did Sophronius, as Maximus reports in his letter to John the chamberlain (or in the book against the Severians), act otherwise as bishop of Africa with the prefect: he referred to the bishop of Rome and to that of Constantinople, that by the will and counsel of both they might restrain the monks of the Severian doctrine. It is great and holy that the bishop of Constantinople should have taught emperor and court; but greater and holier that the bishop of Rome should teach the catholic Church by the mouth of Peter.

Pyrrhus's labour here aimed to draw Maximus to assent to a single operation in Christ, and to take him in by guile, as Sergius (printed 'Surgius') had imposed on Honorius. Accepit Maximus quo pacto Vulg. et reliqui fere interpretes, de ipso ejus filio, nempe regis Moab; qui ferali ea victima litandum Deo, dum extreme laborat, putaverit: forte etiam Abrahami exemplo, qui filii immolatione tentata, etsi non peracta, tantopere Deo placuerit: quod ita sensit R. Peræque tamen Græca vox αὐτοῦ, suum reddatur, referendo ad regem Moab, et ejus, referendo ad regem Edom, in quem facta irruptione rex Moab cum septingentis delectis suis, ad ipsum quidem non pervenerit, ejus tamen primogenitum ceperit, sicque super muros jugulaverit et incenderit; vel cum jam eum in captivis haberet; cujus etiam liberandi causa pater sociale bellum cum regibus Juda et Israel inierit: ejusque dissolvendæ societatis, ipsa hæc dira cædes et immanitas illi causa exstiterit, conversa ejus facinoris invidia in eos, qui belli auctores exstitissent, et ad eas angustias regem Moab redegissent. Hebr. perinde ambigua [Hebrew: את־בנו] filium suum, vel ejus: quo altero modo Pagn., Malvend., Munster, etc., interpretati sunt. Sic etiam qui Am. II, 1, incensa Idumææ regis ossa usque ad cineres, cujus rei causa sic Deus Moabitis comminatur, de hac cæde et holocausto exponunt; quorum sententiam parum pulsant rationes Santii, inque illis hæc potissima, quod rex dicatur illo Anios, cum IV Regum primogenitus regis solum appelletur, quod ad regis titulum non sufficit, ac nisi pater jam in eum jura regni transtulerat. Nam et hoc intellexerunt οἱ LXX, ὃς ἐβασίλευσε, quibus reddiderunt, ὃν ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ' αὐτοῦ, quem sui loco regem constituerat; vel, ut codex Alex. ὃς ἐβασίλευσε, qui ipse regnum capessiverat. Proinde quod Hebr. futuri temporis est, pro præterito positum intellexere. Quod item de ossibus ad cineres usque combustis exaggerat propheta, haud necesse trahere ad ossa e sepulcro effossa, cum nihil occurrat in Scriptura, quo referri possit ea tumuli ossiumque violatio; sed potest intelligi, sic in cineres et favillam redactum hujus principis corpus, relato de eo holocausto, ut nec ossa superfuerint, uti se fere habebant Romanorum ac gentium aliarum busta. In hac itaque satis probabili expositione non satis faveat istud exemplum Maximi scopo; velut scilicet divino instinctu, ad præfigurandum Christi mysterium, quasi piaculari hostia, sic captum hostem rex Moab holocausto obtulerit, eaque victima a se iram depulerit: quomodo etiamnum barbari Canadenses et alii hostes immolant, eorumque laute carnibus epulantur, nullo certe divino instinctu, quo sic mala depellenda intelligant, sed ferina immanitate, ac diabolo instigante, qui sic humano delectetur cruore, Deumque olim æmuletur, nec ignobiliori quam humana sibi hostia, quibus impetrare possit, fieri velit. Christi sacrificium varie Deus in animalium victimis adumbravit; in hominum, nunquam, præterquam in uno Abrahamo et Isaaco, ad usque duntaxat propositi animi manifestationem. Et in ipso Christo victima fuit, quod se ipse obtulit, Judæorum malitia utens, nec tormenta abnuens, ut divinæ satis justitiæ fieret, non velut ipse seipsum interficiens, quod fecere gentilium quidam, nihil prorsus affini Christo exemplo, sed diabolico plane commento.

unplaced.en: On 'his son.' Maximus has taken it, as the Vulgate and nearly all other interpreters do, of his own son, namely the king of Moab's: he thought that in his extremity he must placate God with this deadly victim, perhaps also following the example of Abraham, who pleased God so greatly by the attempted, though uncompleted, sacrifice of his son; so R. Sal. understood it. Yet the Greek word autou may be rendered 'his own,' referring to the king of Moab, or 'of him,' referring to the king of Edom: against whom the king of Moab made a sortie with seven hundred picked men, did not reach him, but captured his firstborn and killed and burned him on the walls; or [it means] when he already had him among his captives, for whose release the father had begun a joint war with the kings of Judah and Israel, and this dreadful slaughter and cruelty became the cause of dissolving the alliance, the hatred of the deed turning on those who had been the authors of the war and had driven the king of Moab into such straits. The Hebrew is likewise ambiguous, 'his son' or 'of him'; Pagninus, Malvenda, Munster and others have interpreted it the second way. So too those who explain Amos 2:1 (the bones of the king of Edom burned to ashes, for which cause God so threatens the Moabites) of this slaughter and burnt offering; the arguments of Sanctius scarcely overthrow their view, chiefly that the man is called king in Amos, while 4 Kings calls him only the king's firstborn, which does not suffice for the title of king unless the father had already transferred the rights of the kingdom to him. For the Septuagint also understood this, 'who reigned,' which they rendered 'whom he had made king in his place'; or, as Codex Alexandrinus has it, 'who himself had taken the kingdom.' Hence they understood the Hebrew future as put for the past. As for the bones burned to ashes which the prophet exaggerates, there is no need to draw this to bones dug up from a tomb, since nothing in Scripture suggests such a violation of tomb and bones; it can rather be understood that this prince's body, once the burnt offering was made of him, was reduced to ashes and cinders so that not even bones remained, as the burial pyres of the Romans and other nations generally were. In this fairly probable explanation, the example does not much favour Maximus's aim: namely that, as by divine instinct to prefigure the mystery of Christ, the king of Moab offered the captured enemy as a burnt offering, like an expiatory victim, and so turned wrath from himself; just as barbarous Canadians and other peoples still sacrifice enemies and feast richly on their flesh, certainly with no divine instinct by which they might suppose evils are to be averted, but from savage cruelty, at the devil's instigation, who delights in human blood and once vied with God, and would not have them offer him a lesser victim than a human one by which they might obtain what they seek. God foreshadowed Christ's sacrifice in various ways in animal victims; in men never, save only in Abraham and Isaac, and then only up to the manifestation of the intention. And in Christ himself there was a victim, in that he offered himself, using the malice of the Jews and not refusing torments, so that divine justice might be satisfied, and not as one killing himself, as some of the heathen did -- an example wholly unlike Christ, and plainly a diabolical invention.

unplaced.en: To Cyrisicius. This heading seems not to be free of error, as it is entitled. Might it be 'to Cyzicinus,' that is, to John, bishop of Cyzicus, to whom the next second and third letters are addressed, with a plainly similar subject; although there the place of his see is not mentioned and he is addressed only as John the bishop? Or are this letter and the following addressed to the bishop of Constantinople himself, from whom he asks to be recalled to him, if only the fear of enemies has gone? Maximus seems to have changed his residence again and again, not only when he went to Africa for fear of the Persians but also on other occasions, so that it is unclear to which bishop's presence he asks, in one letter and another, to be restored. Nactus vero ejus opera cam epistolam, omnem excussi scrupulum; mendo ipso clare deprehenso, ac legendum παραθετική, hoc est, συστατική, Commendatitia scilicet epistola, pro Georgio Africæ præfecto, cum is incerto eventu Constantinopolim evocatus esset. Joannes cubicularius, quasi scilicet sacri cubiculi præfectus, magnæ auctoritatis in aula erat, idem Maximi perquam amicus, ad quem ille pleraque et propria et communia referebat. Quæ sequitur, ipsa ejusdem argumenti est, mirasque ambæ Georgii laudes continent, quas Maximus æmulorum calumniis opponit: quibus tandem vir tantus oppressus, defectionem fecit, dataque semel Vandalis occasione, ab eis Africam liberare non potuit.
unplaced.anchorLine: περὶ θετικῆς (n).
unplaced.en: On 'Peri thetikes.' I had put this down as the title when I received it from the very learned abbot Bigot at Florence, and he had himself read nothing but the title in haste. Having got the letter itself through his work, I removed every doubt: the error was plainly detected, and one must read paratheitke, that is sustatike, a commendatory letter, for George, prefect of Africa, when he had been summoned to Constantinople with an uncertain outcome. John the chamberlain, as being prefect of the sacred bedchamber, was a man of great authority at court, and a very close friend of Maximus, to whom Maximus reported most of his private and common affairs. The letter that follows is of the same subject, and both contain wonderful praises of George, which Maximus sets against the slanders of his rivals; by whom at length so great a man was overwhelmed, made his revolt, and, once he had given the Vandals the opportunity, could not free Africa from them.
